questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Other

questions.question: Please explain: *
questions.answer: I wanted to experience a different university environment and get the exchange experience of getting to know another culture. I also wanted to experience London.

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I had planned to go outside Europe for my exchange, but the corona situation made it difficult. Then I heard about Royal Holloway, and since it was one of the last possibilities to go to UK as part of Erasmus, I thought it made sense to go. I also thought that the university looked very beautiful and I liked the idea of trying to live at campus.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: The communication with Royal Holloway staff was not at all easy. I had to call them several times and it took a long time before they replied to my emails, if at all. Once I got there they were incredibly helpful, but leading up to the arrival and during the application process, it was quite frustrating.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The staff were very good at welcoming us and make sure all was good. There were good possibilities to meet up with support staff physically to help with Learning Agreements and module selections. There is also a Welcome Week the first week of term (where there are no classes) which is a really nice "buffer" to have the time to sort out all the practicalities.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There was the option to stay at either Kingswood or Founder's Hall. Kingswood is about 15-20 minutes away by bus and Founder's is on campus. They are the only two halls available to exchange students. I stayed at Founder's. I would definitely reccommend staying at Founder's as opposed to Kingswood, since those living there had to take the bus all the time. Most of the activities and social life takes place on campus, so it was very nice being so close to it all by living at Founder's.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: There was a little pantry (a room with two microwaves), so it wasn't really possible to cook your own meal. There are several cantinas and a dining hall where I had the most of my food. You get a 50% discount on food from the dining hall when living on campus, which makes the prize alright (around 3 pounds/30kr for a meal).

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: The rooms are not extravagant and not particularly pretty. Founder's is very nice on the outside and a bit old on the inside. I thought it was ok since the stay was only 3-4 months anyway. I liked it because it meant I was close to campus, my classes and all the other exchange students living on campus. Those living off campus definitely had a harder time socially, since Egham (where the university is) is a small town. Because it is about 40 min by train from London, you don't really have the opportunity to go there all the time and be social, so most of the social life will be on campus. So yeah, I would definitely reccommend that you stay on campus if you go to Royal Holloway, to get the full experience.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The housing is a bit expensive, but it was easy to just get housing through the uni rather than try to find something else that is cheaper. Also housing there is just generally a bit expensive.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The updated course lists were not published when I had to apply, so my selections were made based on old lists. This meant that I had to re-do my course selection once I arrived and found out I had too many ECTS-points. I had to go physically several times to get my registrations through, so it wasn't the best system.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: When you apply you write what modules you want. Then the uni writes and tells you if you can get the courses. Once you arrive you probably have to make some adjustments, since there might be timetable clashes, a module isn't running or because it is a course that runs the entire year.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There were several helpdesks, so it all worked out. But a bit frustrating when you don't know what modules you are doing a week before you have to start.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The academic approach is quite different in my opinion, so as a comparative literature student, I felt like I could do well in most modules somewhat related to the humanities. Don't do the CEDAS courses (courses meant for exchange students to improve their english level and knowledge of uk) since the level is not very high and as a Danish student you will probably be bored. Also the workload in CEDAS courses seemed high compared to the courses I was doing. So I would reccommend just going for the courses you think sound interesting. There are 3 "levels" of courses, level 1, 2 and 3 (for first, second and third years). I think most Danish students would find level 1 courses too unacademic. I had 3 level 2 and 1 level 3 course, which I thought was a nice combination.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The programme covered a lot of different things, but to be honest the level was not as high as at KU. I found the modules to be more about reading a text/watching a movie/looking at a piece of art and then just talking about your immediate thoughts rather than applying theory and secondary material. It meant that I had a lot of opportunity to use my time on what I found interesting in the classes and explore, but I didn't feel challenged by the academic level.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: As said, the level was lower than in Denmark, but on the other hand I really enjoyed the opportunity to explore the things/art/literature/movies I found interesting. They don't expect you to be super prepared for the classes.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I had a mix of lectures and seminars. There was a lot less group work at Royal Holloway and more open class discussion. The teacher would often pose a question or ask what we thought, and then you just had to speak your opinion. I didn't always love the style of teaching since it became a bit of a monologue from the teacher and a bit repetitive. But individual teacher were very great.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Queer Histories
Horror Cinema in the Hispanic World
Gender and Clothing in the 20th Century Literature and Culture
International Film: Readings and Representations

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I really enjoyed Horror Cinema in the Hispanic World with professor Dr. Camilo Chiappe Bejar. It was really fun to watch different horror movies and talk about what was scary and how they functioned. My other courses were also very nice and interesting, but the Horror Cinema was my favourite.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I had to pay for an expensive corona test upon arrival (the uk system is really bad with entry tests, can be very expensive, so watch out). I also had to get a student visa because of Brexit.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food was a bit more expensive than I thought. It quickly adds up when you don't have the possibility to ever cook yourself and have to buy everything.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There were SO many societies that you could join. Imagine an American highschool. There was a huge fair with all the different clubs, sports and societies in the beginning of term (I think there is like over 100 different to choose from). Definitely join something or go to some of the events! It's a great way to meet new people.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Like I said, so much! I joined the Dance Society and the Craft Society. Also considered the Harry Potter society or Tennis, but you have to be selective because you don't have time for all of them.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Join the trips to other UK cities that the Student Union hosts. They generally make a lot of events that you should definitely join, especially in the first few weeks where you will likely meet the most of your friends. I mostly hung out with other exchange students and it was very nice to go to eg. Brighton with them. There are also a lot of parties. But probably join a sports society! I really liked the Dance Society

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Of course go to London when you can, it's very nice to be so close to it. But I would also recommend visiting Windsor, which is very close by.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Once you get used to talking English all the time, it is very nice. People are very friendly and talkative, especially in the beginning of term. A lot of the students at UK universities are a bit younger than in the DK (a lot are around 19) so you might struggle a bit with feeling a bit old and having to socialize with people who just moved out from their parents. But hang out with the exchange students who are often a little older and you will be fine. Everyone just wants to get new friends and be sociable so just throw yourself into it and you'll find friends easily.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: In the first week of term there is the Welcome Week. It's basically an entire week only meant for socializing. Go to as much as you can, because this is the time where you can meet people. Go to the events for international/exchange students to meet them, and go to the different "taster" sessions for the societies. In general just spend the first weeks socialising and making connections and don't worry too much about the classes.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: British people are very polite and good at small talk in my experience, so it was a bit challenging to have so many "how are you" conversations in the beginning. But I found that once I just let go and tried to relax in it I really enjoyed it.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I liked that it's so easy and normal to go to the pub with a few friends after class, just for a beer or a cider. I also think that there is a lot more room for differences compared to Copenhagen. A lot of people experimented with their hair and appearances, and there was a large focus on making sure that there was a space for LGBT people and people of color and making campus inclusive, which I found very comforting and welcoming.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Dont' expect to have your exchange in London - it's not. You will live in Egham and your experience will be more like living (if at Founder's) on a castle (a bit like Hogwarts) with people a bit younger than you. So don't go because you want the metropolitan London-vibe, but because you want to have a fun time and try out the British university experience living on campus.

Also, the term is shorter than the Danish semester, so it's a bit short the exchange (2,5 months). It's a bit short, but for me it was nice since you get a great experience but don't have to be there for 6 months.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: No I think I covered it all.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: I loved living at the castle and campus. It is a very beautiful area. I also really enjoyed just having the time to focus on the things that interested me personally and academically and meeting people from all over the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Not having your own kitchen and not really having a relaxing social space that is not your bedroom. I missed having a living room where I could hang out with friends etc. You are very "out there" all the time and have to interact with people you run into at campus all the time. It was nice at times but also a little exhausting in the long run.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: All in all, I really enjoyed my time at Royal Holloway. I thought I was going for an urban experience and living in London exploring the city, but it was more living on a micro-verse on campus and living very close with your friends. It was not what I had expected but I ended up being so happy that I tried this experience with all the societies and the university community that is just SO different from the university community at KU.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
